name: Carlos Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Portuguese into English for import businesses, mostly supplier contracts, invoices and product specs for coffee roasters and furniture importers who buy from Brazil. I put everything through two AI tools, compare them, and then check the clauses that matter, like payment terms and delivery dates. Some days I'm on calls interpreting between a roaster and a farm cooperative in Minas Gerais. I rent a one-bedroom flat ten minutes from my dad's hardware shop, and I still help there on Saturdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the business side, honestly, seeing how a deal comes together. I'm junior and my legal Portuguese still has gaps, but the tools help and I learn fast. What wears me out is chasing invoices from small clients who pay in sixty days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool for people who work hard, and that the hype was mostly marketing. I'd post about how I use it to help small firms. I'd be upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's fine for me. I'm already faster than people who don't use the tools, and small importers want someone they can call. My income would grow as I add clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up two or three more importers and offer a monthly retainer instead of per-job pricing. I'd invest about two hundred a month in an index fund. I'd also do a short course in contract law for translators, about four hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Keen, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a monthly retainer. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because chasing invoices is killing me. A retainer means steady money, and the client gets a person on call. My dad runs his shop on regular customers, and I'd like the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad think of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks I sit at a computer all day, which I do. He'd rather I sold hammers. But my dad is proud when I tell him I helped a roaster buy a whole container of beans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small businesses, and I'd offer to help them use it. I'd say government should get out of the way. I'd be confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, plain translation goes, but small firms need someone to run AI for them and check contracts. I could be that person, maybe with a small agency. I think I'd earn more, though it's a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a small agency offering AI translation plus human checks for importers, and hire one part-time checker. I'd spend about a thousand on setup, website and insurance. I'd keep my savings at four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a gamble. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big firms could offer the same thing cheaper. Or the AI could get so good that importers don't need me to check. I'd be watching closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would your first hire be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend from university, Ana, who's better at legal Portuguese than me. I'd pay her per contract. She'd keep me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, but people should work, not wait for handouts. I'd say families should help each other. I'd still be upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my agency would last maybe a year. If AI does all thinking work, importers won't need me to check contracts. The shop is the only thing I have that's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next two years building the agency and saving hard, maybe five hundred a month. I'd talk to my dad about taking over the hardware shop and modernising it. After it arrives, I'd be behind the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Excited, still, but alarmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad's hardware shop. Would robots replace that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031, maybe. But a hardware shop is about advice and trust, because people ask which screw to use. I'd hope they'd still want a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be thrilled. He's been asking me to take over for years. I'd just be doing it for a different reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something real. I'd tell young people to start businesses. I'd be confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me three good years of agency income. Then I'd move to the shop. It's a decent plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the agency for three years, saving and investing. I'd then take over the shop around 2030. I'd put money into making the shop online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Online shop. Isn't that thinking work that AI would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd use AI to run the online shop, but the counter and the advice would be me. That's the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you marry or settle down in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to. My mum keeps asking. Maybe once the shop is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and people should use it. I'd say businesses should train their own people. I'd be optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd build the agency, make money, then take over the shop. I'd be in a strong position. I feel good about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the agency for six years, hire two more people, and save. Around 2033 I'd move to the shop. I'd keep investing steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at most. Mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Hire two more. Isn't that a risk when AGI is coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but for six years they'd earn well. I'd be honest with my staff about the end date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not learning legal Portuguese properly. But honestly, I'd rather be good at business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the agency wouldn't have time to pay off. What would help is cheap business loans and fewer rules for small firms. I don't want handouts, I want room to build.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I learn from my dad. My dad's hardware shop taught me more about business than university did.

headlineQuote: My dad's hardware shop taught me more about business than university did.
portrait: A **27-year-old** Portuguese–English translator for import businesses who uses AI tools every day.
Wants to build a **small agency** running AI translation with human checks.
Feels **calm** in AI Plateau and sees opportunity in Steady Disruption.
Plans to take over his dad's **hardware shop** as his hands-on fallback.
Prefers **business freedom** and family help over state support.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, before the agency can pay off.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans** and fewer rules for small firms.
